title: The king who did not seek
sum: After nine chapters of names, the story opens on Mount Gilboa. The Philistines rout Israel, Saul's sons fall, and Saul, wounded by archers, falls on his own sword. The Philistines strip his body, send his head and armor around their land, and fix his skull in Dagon's temple. The brave men of Jabesh-gilead bury the bones and fast for seven days.

Almost all of this is copied from 1 Samuel 31. Then Chronicles adds its own verdict: Saul died for his unfaithfulness, because he did not keep the LORD's word, consulted a ghost and did not seek the LORD. So the LORD turned the kingdom over to David. Saul's whole reign is reduced to a warning, and the book's great theme, seeking God, is announced through the king who failed to do it.
readings: Saul's last battle in the Jezreel Valley, about 1010 BC, is told with the same facts as in Samuel. The Philistines controlled the valley and the road to Beth-shan, and their victory left Israel's north open. Chronicles' small differences, such as Dagon's temple and the oak at Jabesh, may come from another form of the Samuel story or from the Chronicler's shortening.

Chronicles uses Saul as the first example of a pattern it will repeat for every king of Judah: those who seek the LORD prosper, and those who act unfaithfully fall. The word ma'al, "unfaithfulness," ties Saul's death to the exile itself (9:1), so the first king's fall foreshadows the nation's.

views.H: Traditional readers take the chapter as a true record of Saul's death and God's judgment, with Chronicles adding the inspired explanation that Samuel's narrative implies (1 Samuel 13:13–14; 1 Samuel 15:23; 1 Samuel 28:6).
views.C: Critical scholars see the Chronicler beginning his history where his interest begins, with David, and using Saul only as a dark foil. His closing verdict shows his doctrine of immediate retribution in its sharpest form.
views.S: Chapter 10 is the first and closest of the parallels: compare 1 Samuel 31 line by line. The changes are few but telling: "his whole house" for "all his men," no Beth-shan wall, no burning, Dagon instead of the Ashtaroth, and two new verses of judgment.
views.J: Jewish tradition is divided on Saul, honoring his courage in going to his last battle knowing he would die (1 Samuel 28:19) while accepting the verdict of 10:13–14. Some rabbinic voices list his sins as the slaughter of Nob and the sparing of Agag.
views.X: Christian readers have often read Saul as a warning about a faith that begins well and ends in disobedience, and they have read the transfer of the kingdom to David as one step toward the Son of David.

deep.b: Reading 1 Samuel 31 and 1 Chronicles 10 side by side is the best introduction to the method of Chronicles. Most sentences match. Where they differ, three kinds of change appear: simplifying (no night march, no burning, the Jezreel valley alone), sharpening ("his whole house died"), and explaining (10:13–14). Readers who know only one account miss what the other is saying. The site's Plain aims to use the same English as 1 Samuel 31 wherever the Hebrew is the same, so that the differences show up on the page: compare "to bring the good news to their idols" (10:9) with Samuel's "their idols' temples."

Chronicles builds its whole story around two verbs, darash, "seek," and ma'al, "act unfaithfully." Saul is the king who did not ask of the LORD (10:14, where the Plain renders darash "ask"). David's first act will be to seek the ark (13:3). David will tell Solomon that whoever seeks God will find him (see 28:9), and the promise to Solomon sums up the whole idea: if God's people humble themselves, pray and seek his face, he will forgive and heal their land (2 Chronicles 7:14). The verdict on Saul is harsh, but it is the negative image of the book's hope.

echoes: 1 Samuel 31:1–13; 1 Samuel 28:3–25; 1 Samuel 13:13–14; 1 Samuel 15:22–28; 2 Samuel 1:17–27; 1 Chronicles 9:1; 2 Chronicles 7:14

settings.when: After the account of Saul's death on Mount Gilboa
settings.why: Not a speech in the story but the writer's own judgment. Saul died for 'unfaithfulness' (ma'al): he did not keep the LORD's word, he consulted a ghost, and he 'did not ask the LORD.' These are the key words of the whole book. For readers who knew the exile as the result of unfaithfulness (9:1), Saul's end was a first lesson: seek the LORD, or lose the kingdom.

title: All Israel makes David king
sum: All Israel comes to Hebron, reminds David that the LORD called him to shepherd his people, and the elders anoint him king, as the LORD had said through Samuel. At once David marches on Jebus. The Jebusites boast that he will never get in, but he takes the fortress of Zion; Joab leads the attack and becomes commander. David builds the city, Joab restores it, and David grows greater because the LORD of Armies is with him.

Then comes the roll of David's warriors: the Three, the Thirty and their feats, from Jashobeam's spear to the water from Bethlehem's well, poured out to the LORD. The list follows 2 Samuel 23 and adds sixteen more names.

views.H: Traditional readers see the coronation and the capture of Jerusalem as the founding of the kingdom God promised, with the heroes as real men whose deeds were remembered in court lists.
views.C: Critical scholars note that Chronicles erases seven years of civil war (2 Samuel 2–4) and moves the hero list from the end of David's reign to its start, to show a united Israel behind David from the first day. Many still regard the hero list itself as old and valuable.
views.S: Compare 11:1–9 with 2 Samuel 5:1–10 (David's age and the blind and the lame are missing; Joab's promotion is new) and 11:10–41 with 2 Samuel 23:8–39 (a skipped line in 11:13, a dozen spellings, and 11:41–47 added).
views.J: Jewish tradition remembers the water from Bethlehem as a model of a king who refused to profit from his men's danger. Rabbinic readers sometimes took the story of the well as a figure for David's longing for Torah, or for a ruling of law that his men brought him (Bavli Bava Kamma 60b).
views.X: Christians have read David's pouring out the water as an image of self-giving, and the capture of Zion as the beginning of the city that becomes, in the New Testament, a picture of God's people (Hebrews 12:22).

deep.h: How Chronicles uses the hero list
deep.b: In 2 Samuel 23 the list of David's warriors sits in an appendix, after David's last words. Chronicles brings it forward and wraps it in a new frame: these chiefs "stood firmly with him in his kingship, to make him king" (11:10). The list then flows into chapter 12, where more and more men join David, from Ziklag to Hebron, until "all the rest of Israel too was of one heart to make David king" (12:38). The heroes are no longer only famous fighters; they are the first circle of a whole people choosing the LORD's king.

This chapter is a classroom for textual criticism. Chronicles helps repair Samuel ("he swung his spear," 11:11; Pas-dammim, 11:13), and Samuel helps repair Chronicles (the lost line about Shammah in 11:13; Elika in 11:27). Neither book is a perfect copy. Comparing the two is how scholars rebuild the text, and how readers can see that the Bible's copyists, for all their care, were human.

echoes: 2 Samuel 5:1–10; 2 Samuel 23:8–39; 1 Samuel 16:1–13; 1 Samuel 22:1–2; Joshua 15:63; Judges 1:21; Psalm 2:6; Hebrews 12:22

settings.what: All Israel's offer to David and the covenant at Hebron
settings.by: All Israel; then David and the elders
settings.to: David at Hebron; and the LORD, before whom the covenant was made
settings.why: 'We are your own bone and flesh.' The tribes recall David's leadership and the LORD's word that he would shepherd Israel, and the elders make a covenant with him. Chronicles skips the seven years of civil war (2 Samuel 2–4) so that all Israel comes at once. For readers in Yehud, the scene pictured the unity of all the tribes around David's house that they hoped for.

settings.what: David pours out the water from Bethlehem
settings.to: His men at the stronghold, and God
settings.when: While a Philistine post held Bethlehem
settings.why: David longs for water from Bethlehem's well, and three warriors risk their lives to bring it. He pours it out to the LORD: 'Am I to drink the blood of these men?' The act honors his men's lives as too precious to spend on his wish. Chronicles puts the story at the head of the warrior list, near the start of David's reign. It is a picture of a king who gives to God what his people give him.

title: A camp like the camp of God
sum: This chapter is Chronicles' own. It names the men who came over to David while Saul still lived: Benjaminite archers and slingers, Saul's own kin; Gadites who crossed the flooded Jordan, with faces like lions; men of Benjamin and Judah, to whom Amasai, clothed by the Spirit, swore loyalty; men of Manasseh who joined David when the Philistines sent him home.

Then it counts the army that came to Hebron "to turn Saul's kingdom over to him": every tribe, from Judah and Simeon to the tribes east of the Jordan, more than three hundred forty thousand men, of one heart. They feast for three days, with food brought from as far as Naphtali, and Israel is full of joy.
readings: Some scholars think the Chronicler had real lists of David's early supporters, drawn from tribal or military records. The detail of the Benjaminite slingers, the Gadite crossing and the Manassite defectors fits the world of 1 Samuel 22–30.
Read as a picture of all Israel

Others read the chapter as the Chronicler's portrait of what Israel should be: every tribe, north and south, gathered around David's house with a whole heart. For his small community in Judah, it was a call to see themselves as part of a larger Israel that still belonged to David's line.

views.H: Traditional readers take the lists as genuine records showing that David's rise was supported across Israel long before Saul's death.
views.C: Critical scholars generally treat the tribal numbers as idealized and the chapter as a composition of the Chronicler, though they allow that some names may be old.
views.S: Nothing here is in Samuel, but it fits Samuel's story at many points: Ziklag (1 Samuel 27), the Philistine march (1 Samuel 29), the Amalekite raid (1 Samuel 30), and the seven years at Hebron (2 Samuel 2–5).
views.J: The men of Issachar "who knew how to read the times" (12:32) became a byword in Jewish tradition for scholars of the calendar and of Torah, and the verse is still quoted for wisdom about one's own age.
views.X: Christians have read Amasai's Spirit-inspired pledge (12:18) as a model of loyalty to the coming Son of David, and the gathering at Hebron as a picture of the nations coming to Christ's kingdom.

deep.b: The tribal totals (12:24–37) add up to more than 340,000. Readers take them literally, as counts of units (the Hebrew elef can mean a clan or company), or as the Chronicler's way of saying "everyone." One detail is worth noticing: the largest numbers come not from Judah but from the far tribes, Zebulun, Asher, Naphtali and the tribes beyond the Jordan. Whatever the numbers mean, the chapter is not boasting about Judah.

deep.title: Claude's theory: three circles around the king
deep.b: My own reading of chapters 11–12: the Chronicler shows David made king in three widening circles. First the elders anoint him at Hebron (11:3). Then the inner circle of heroes "stood firmly with him" (11:10–47). Then the whole people, tribe by tribe, comes "with a whole heart" (12:23–40). Between the heroes and the tribes, he places the men who came while David was still an outlaw (12:1–22), so the circles widen through time as well as space. The pattern resembles the way Chronicles later gathers priests, Levites, leaders and all Israel around Solomon (28:1; 29:1–9). Scholars such as Williamson have analyzed chapter 12's careful structure; seeing 11–12 as three circles is my own proposal.

echoes: 1 Samuel 22:1–2; 1 Samuel 27:1–7; 1 Samuel 29:1–11; 1 Samuel 30:1–20; 2 Samuel 2:1–4; 2 Samuel 5:1–3; Judges 20:16; Judges 6:34

settings.by: David; then Amasai, chief of the Thirty, clothed by the Spirit
settings.to: Men of Benjamin and Judah who came to David's fortress
settings.when: While David was still an outlaw from Saul
settings.why: David asks if they come in peace. Amasai answers in a short poem: 'Peace, peace to you, and peace to whoever helps you, for your God has helped you.' The Spirit-given words declare that God is with David even before he is king. Readers heard a word about loyalty: those who join David's cause are on God's side.

settings.what: The muster of the tribes at Hebron
settings.when: At David's coronation over all Israel
settings.why: Every tribe, including the Levites and the far northern tribes, sends its men to Hebron 'with a whole heart, to make David king.' The great numbers and the three-day feast picture all Israel united and joyful. For a later community divided between Yehud and Samaria, it was a vision of what Israel had been and could be.
views: Some scholars think the lists come from real musters, with numbers later enlarged or misread ('thousand' as 'unit').
Others read the passage as the Chronicler's ideal of all Israel gathered around David.

title: Uzzah and the ark
sum: David's first act as king is to consult the assembly about the ark of God, neglected all through Saul's reign. All Israel, from Shihor in Egypt to Lebo-hamath, gathers to bring it from Kiriath-jearim. They load it on a new cart and set off with all their strength and with songs. At Chidon's threshing floor the oxen stumble, Uzzah reaches out to steady the ark, and the LORD strikes him dead.
David is angry and afraid. He leaves the ark at the house of Obed-edom the Gittite, and for three months the LORD blesses Obed-edom's household and everything he has.

views.H: Traditional readers see a lesson in God's holiness: even good intentions cannot replace obedience to his instructions for approaching him (Numbers 4:15).
views.C: Critical scholars see an old story behind the place name Perez-uzzah, which the Chronicler explains in his own way: the failure was a failure to seek God "the way the ruling requires" (15:13).
views.S: Compare 2 Samuel 6:1–11. Chronicles adds the assembly (13:1–5), moves the episode before David's palace and wars, follows a Samuel text like 4QSam-a at Baalah and "strength and songs," and states plainly why Uzzah died.
views.J: The Talmud (Sotah 35a) blames David for forgetting that the ark must be carried on the shoulder, and links the lapse to his calling God's laws "songs" (Psalm 119:54). Uzzah's death became a classic warning against treating holy things casually.
views.X: Christian readers have contrasted the untouchable ark with Jesus, who touched the unclean and was touched by them, while still drawing from this chapter the warning that God's holiness is never to be taken lightly (Hebrews 12:28–29).

deep.b: Samuel tells the first attempt to move the ark after David has built his palace and beaten the Philistines. Chronicles puts it first, right after Jerusalem is taken. The result is a clear sequence: David seeks the ark (13), the attempt fails because it was not done God's way, and in the three months of waiting God blesses both Obed-edom's house and David's (13:14; 14:1–17). Then David tries again, this time with the Levites (15). For Chronicles' readers, who had rebuilt the Temple and its worship, the lesson was practical: zeal is not enough; worship must follow what God has commanded.

deep.title: Claude's theory: from Israel's breaking out to God's
deep.b: Commentators on Chronicles, such as Sara Japhet, Ralph Klein and Martin Selman, have long noted that the root parats, "break out," runs through the ark story: the LORD's "breakout" against Uzzah and the name Perez-uzzah (13:11), Baal-perazim, where God bursts through the Philistines (14:11), and David's words to the Levites that the LORD "burst out against us" (15:13). The site's 2 Samuel page reads the same root in 2 Samuel 5–6. My own small addition is the first link in the chain. David's opening call, "let us send word out everywhere" (13:2), uses the same verb (literally "let us break out"), so the story may move from Israel's eager, careless breaking out, to God's breaking out in judgment, and then to God breaking through for those who obey. Whether the Chronicler meant 13:2 as part of the pattern is uncertain, since the verb there has its ordinary sense.

echoes: 2 Samuel 6:1–11; 1 Samuel 6:1–7:2; Numbers 4:1–20; Numbers 7:9; Joshua 15:9; Leviticus 10:1–3; Hebrews 12:28–29

settings.what: David's proposal to bring up the ark
settings.to: The whole assembly of Israel, after counsel with the commanders
settings.when: Soon after David became king of all Israel
settings.why: David asks the assembly to gather everyone, including the priests and Levites, and bring back the ark: 'In the days of Saul we did not seek it.' The king leads by consent, and his first act is to restore worship. For readers who gathered as the 'assembly' at the second Temple, the scene modeled how worship is renewed.

title: Blessing on David's house
sum: While the ark waits with Obed-edom, blessing comes to David. Hiram king of Tyre sends cedar and craftsmen to build him a house, and David understands that the LORD has set him firmly in place for the good of his people. He takes more wives and has thirteen sons in Jerusalem, Solomon among them.

Twice the Philistines raid the Valley of Rephaim, and twice David asks God before he fights. At Baal-perazim God bursts through the enemy like a flood, and the Philistines' gods are burned. The second time God tells David to circle behind them and wait for the sound of marching in the treetops. David's name goes out to every land.

views.H: Traditional readers see the chapter as God's blessing on a king who asks him before acting, in contrast to Saul (10:13–14).
views.C: Critical scholars note that the Chronicler has rearranged Samuel's material so that the blessing of 14:1–17 falls between the two attempts to move the ark, as God's answer to David's zeal.
views.S: Compare 2 Samuel 5:11–25. Chronicles leaves out the concubines, keeps the Baal name Beeliada, burns the Philistine idols instead of carrying them off, and adds 14:17.
views.J: Jewish readers have noted that David asks God even when victory seems certain, and that the second battle is won by waiting for God's signal rather than by David's skill.
views.X: Christian readers have heard in the sound of marching in the treetops a picture of God going before his people, and in the burning of the idols the call to put away false gods.

echoes: 2 Samuel 5:11–25; 1 Chronicles 3:5–9; Isaiah 28:21; Deuteronomy 7:5; Deuteronomy 7:25; Matthew 1:6; Luke 3:31

settings.what: David asks God before the first battle
settings.when: When the Philistines raided the Valley of Rephaim
settings.why: David asks before he fights, and God answers, 'Go up.' This is what Saul did not do (10:14). The exchange shows readers that David's success came from seeking God.

Do not attack head on; wait for the sound of marching in the treetops, 'for God will have gone out ahead of you.' The oracle makes the victory God's own. For readers it was a reminder that their safety depended on listening for God's lead.

title: The ark carried the right way
sum: David prepares a place and a tent for the ark, and this time he declares that only the Levites may carry it. He gathers the priests and six Levite clans, tells them to make themselves holy, and explains the first failure: we did not seek the LORD the way the ruling requires. The Levites carry the ark on their shoulders with poles, as Moses commanded.

David also has the Levite leaders appoint singers and musicians, Heman, Asaph and Ethan with cymbals, others with lyres and harps, and priests with trumpets. With great joy the ark comes up from Obed-edom's house, with sacrifices, shouting and music. David, robed in linen, dances, and Michal, looking down from a window, despises him in her heart.

views.H: Traditional readers see David as the founder of Israel's worship, organizing the Levites according to the law of Moses and the music that would later fill the Temple.
views.C: Critical scholars think the Chronicler projects the Levite orders and singer guilds of the Second Temple back into David's time, while preserving the core of the procession from 2 Samuel 6.
views.S: Nearly everything in 15:1–24 is new. Then compare 15:25–29 with 2 Samuel 6:12–16: seven bulls and seven rams (like 4QSam-a) instead of an ox and a fatling, a linen robe for David where Samuel has whirling, and Michal's contempt without the quarrel.
views.J: Jewish tradition sees here the institution of the Levitical song, which the Mishnah describes as part of the daily Temple service (Mishnah Tamid 7:3–4), and the origin of the psalm headings' musical terms.
views.X: Christians have read the joyful, ordered worship of this chapter as a model for church music, and David's humility before the ark as a contrast with Michal's pride.

deep.b: Readers of the Psalms meet strange words in the headings: alamoth (Psalm 46), sheminith (Psalms 6 and 12) and above all lamnatseach, "for the director," at the head of fifty-five psalms. This chapter is one of the very few places where those words appear in a story (15:20–21). It does not fully explain them, but it shows them in use: groups of Levite players, some with lyres and some with harps, some "to lead." It also introduces the singers named in the Psalm titles, Asaph, Heman and Ethan.

echoes: 2 Samuel 6:12–16; Numbers 4:1–15; Numbers 7:9; Numbers 10:1–10; Exodus 25:12–15; Deuteronomy 10:8; Psalm 46; Psalm 6

settings.what: David's ruling on who may carry the ark
settings.to: All Israel, and especially the Levites
settings.when: Before the second attempt to bring up the ark
settings.why: 'The ark of God is not to be carried by anyone but the Levites.' The ruling applies the law of Moses (Numbers 4:15; Deuteronomy 10:8) after the death of Uzzah. It binds the Levites to their task and keeps others from touching the holy things. For readers it explained why the Levites had their place in the Temple.

settings.what: David's charge to the Levite heads
settings.to: Zadok and Abiathar the priests and the six heads of Levite families
settings.when: Before the ark was brought from Obed-edom's house
settings.why: 'Make yourselves holy... because we did not seek him the way the ruling requires.' David explains the disaster at Perez-uzzah as a failure to follow the law, and tells the Levites to carry the ark on their shoulders as Moses commanded. The charge taught readers that zeal must follow God's ruling.

title: A song of thanks
sum: The ark is set in David's tent. David offers sacrifices, blesses the people and gives every man and woman bread and cakes. He appoints Levites to serve before the ark: to call the LORD to mind, to give thanks and to praise him. Asaph leads with cymbals, and priests blow trumpets.

Then comes the song: a call to give thanks and to remember the covenant with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob and the promise of the land (from Psalm 105); a call to all the earth to praise the LORD as King (from Psalm 96); and a prayer, "Rescue us... gather us... from the nations" (from Psalm 106). David then sets Asaph before the ark in Jerusalem, and Zadok, Heman and Jeduthun at the tabernacle in Gibeon, to keep the daily offerings and the thanksgiving going.
readings: The song shows what the ark's arrival meant: God had kept his covenant, given the land and made Israel safe among the nations, and the right answer was thanksgiving. Traditional readers have often seen David as the one who gave this song to the Levites, whether he wrote it or not.

The song is built from psalms the Chronicler's readers already sang. Its choices fit their world: a small people among the nations, holding on to the land promise and praying to be gathered. In David's day, the Levites sing the hopes of the community after the exile.

views.H: Traditional readers take the chapter as David's institution of regular praise, with the song as an inspired composition or arrangement given to Asaph on the day the ark arrived.
views.C: Most critical scholars hold that the Chronicler composed the song from Psalms 105, 96 and 106, and many date those psalms, at least in their final form, after the exile, which helps date Chronicles.
views.S: Only 16:1–3 and 16:43 come from 2 Samuel 6:17–20. Samuel moves on to Michal's quarrel; Chronicles fills the space with Levites, a psalm and the double sanctuary at Jerusalem and Gibeon.
views.J: Jewish liturgy uses this song: 16:8–36 is recited in the morning service (the Hodu), in the section of Psukei de-Zimra, "verses of song," which shows how deeply it entered Jewish prayer.
views.X: Christians hear in the song's call to the nations (16:23–31) the mission of the gospel to all peoples, and in the coming of the LORD to judge the earth (16:33) a promise of Christ's return.

deep.b: Set the song beside the Psalter: 1 Chronicles 16:8–22 = Psalm 105:1–15; 1 Chronicles 16:23–33 = Psalm 96:1b–13a; 1 Chronicles 16:34–36 = Psalm 106:1, 47–48. The Chronicler stops Psalm 105 before Joseph, Moses and the plagues, and omits the "new song" and the final verse of Psalm 96. He changes "Abraham" to "Israel" (16:13), "he remembers" to "remember!" (16:15), "his sanctuary" to "his place" (16:27) and "his courts" to "his presence" (16:29). He also turns Psalm 106's closing instruction, let all the people say Amen, into a report that they did (16:36). Small as they are, these changes show a writer shaping old songs for a new moment.

deep.title: Claude's theory: a history in a song
deep.b: I suggest that the Chronicler chose and ordered these psalm pieces so that the song retells Israel's story in three stages that match his book. First the patriarchs, few and wandering, protected and promised the land (16:13–22); this matches the genealogies of chapters 1–9. Then the nations called to worship the LORD as King (16:23–33); this matches the kingdom of David and Solomon. Then the prayer to be gathered from among the nations (16:35); this matches the exile and return with which 2 Chronicles ends (2 Chronicles 36:22–23). The song would be a small map of the whole work. Scholars such as Japhet and Williamson have noted how the song addresses the community after the exile; reading it as an outline of Chronicles is my own proposal.

echoes: 2 Samuel 6:17–20; Psalm 105:1–15; Psalm 96:1–13; Psalm 106:1; Psalm 106:47–48; 1 Kings 3:4; 2 Chronicles 1:3–6; Ezra 3:11

settings.by: David, given to Asaph and his kinsmen to sing; made from Psalms 105, 96 and 106
settings.to: The LORD, sung by the Levite singers before the ark, with the whole people answering 'Amen'
settings.when: The day the ark came to its tent in Jerusalem
settings.why: The song calls Israel to give thanks, remember the covenant with Abraham and the gift of the land, and summon all the earth to praise the LORD as King. It ends with a prayer: 'Gather us and pull us out from the nations.' That line does not fit David's day well. It fits the Chronicler's readers, many of whose people were still scattered. They sang these psalms in their own Temple, and here David himself gives them the words.
views: Traditional readers: David gave the Levites this song, whether he composed it or used existing psalms.
Most critical scholars: the Chronicler put together psalms his community sang, choosing lines that spoke to their life among the nations.

title: God will build David a house
sum: Settled in his cedar house, David tells Nathan that the ark is still under curtains, and Nathan tells him to do what is in his heart. That night God's word corrects them both: David is not the one who will build the house. God has never asked for one. Instead, God will build David a house: he will raise up one of David's sons, who will build God a house, and God will be his father, keep his loyal love with him, and establish him in God's own house and kingdom forever.

David goes in, sits before the LORD and prays in wonder: who am I, and what is my house? There is no God like the LORD and no nation like Israel. He asks God to confirm his word, and ends with confidence: you, LORD, have blessed it, and it is blessed forever.

views.H: Traditional Jewish and Christian readers see in this chapter the covenant with David, the root of the hope for a Messiah from his line.
views.C: Critical scholars see the Chronicler rereading Nathan's oracle in the light of Solomon's Temple and of his own time without a king, by turning Samuel's "your house and your kingdom" into "in my house and in my kingdom" (17:14).
views.S: Compare 2 Samuel 7. Chronicles drops Samuel's note that the LORD had given David rest from his enemies (17:1), makes the refusal a statement (17:4), reads "judges" for "tribes" (17:6), drops the rod of correction (17:13), says "in my house and in my kingdom" (17:14) and turns the prayer's last wish into a confident statement (17:27).
views.J: Jewish tradition reads the promise of a lasting throne as the foundation of the messianic hope: a king from David's line who will restore Israel and rebuild the Temple, as Maimonides summarized it in his laws of kings.
views.X: Christians read 17:13–14 as fulfilled in Jesus: the angel promises that God will give him the throne of his father David and that his kingdom will have no end (Luke 1:32–33), and Hebrews quotes the father-son promise of him (Hebrews 1:5).

deep.h: From David's kingdom to God's kingdom
deep.b: Samuel's version promises David that his house and his kingdom will stand before him forever (2 Samuel 7:16). Chronicles' version says that God will make David's son stand in God's house and God's kingdom (17:14). In Chronicles this is not a passing phrase: David says God chose Solomon to sit on the throne of the LORD's kingdom (28:5), Solomon sits on the LORD's throne (29:23), and the kingdom of the LORD is in the hands of David's sons (2 Chronicles 13:8). For readers living under Persian rule, without a king, the change was full of hope: the kingdom had never really belonged to David, and so it had never really ended.

echoes: 2 Samuel 7:1–29; 1 Chronicles 22:6–10; 1 Chronicles 28:2–7; Psalm 89:3–4; Psalm 89:26–37; Psalm 132:11–12; Isaiah 9:6–7; Luke 1:32–33; Acts 2:30; Hebrews 1:5

settings.to: David, in his cedar house in Jerusalem
settings.when: After David settled in his house and wanted to build a house for the ark
settings.why: David will not build the house; God will build David a 'house,' a line of kings. His son will build the Temple, and God will be a father to him and 'make him stand in my house and in my kingdom for all time.' Chronicles changes Samuel's 'your house and your kingdom' (2 Samuel 7:16) so that the kingdom is God's. For readers with no king, the promise meant that God's kingdom still stood, and that it was tied to David's line and the Temple.
views: Williamson and many Christian readers: the promise looks forward to a future son of David.
Fulfilled in Solomon and the Temple
Others: the Chronicler saw the promise fulfilled in Solomon's Temple, and the Temple as the lasting form of God's kingdom.

settings.to: The LORD, as David sat before him
settings.why: 'Who am I?' David answers the promise with wonder, praises God for redeeming Israel, and asks him to make his word sure forever. The prayer teaches readers how to receive a promise: by humble thanks and by asking God to keep it. Its closing words, that God has blessed David's house so that it lasts forever, gave later readers words for their own prayers.

traditions.q: God promises David a son whose throne will stand forever (1 Chronicles 17:11–14). How is the promise kept?
views: The promise will be kept to the letter: Christ will sit on David's throne in Jerusalem and rule over the nation of Israel in a future thousand-year kingdom. Classic dispensationalists say he now sits at the Father's right hand, not yet on David's throne (so the Scofield Reference Bible on 2 Samuel 7). Progressive dispensationalists, such as Darrell Bock and Craig Blaising, say his reign as David's son has already begun, though its full form is still to come.

The promise is being kept now. Peter preached that God raised Jesus to sit on David's throne (Acts 2:30–36), so Christ already reigns as David's son over his church and the world, and his reign will have no end.

Christ is the Son of David whose kingdom will have no end (Luke 1:32–33). His kingdom is already present in mystery in the Church, and will come in its fullness when he returns in glory (Catechism 669, 763).

title: Victory on every side
sum: David beats the Philistines and takes Gath, makes Moab pay tribute, and defeats Hadadezer of Zobah, capturing a thousand chariots. When the Arameans of Damascus come to help, he defeats them and stations troops in their land. He brings Hadadezer's gold shields to Jerusalem, and from Hadadezer's towns he takes the bronze that Solomon will use for the Temple. Tou of Hamath sends gifts, and David dedicates them all to the LORD. Abishai defeats Edom in the Valley of Salt.
The refrain repeats: everywhere David went, the LORD made him win. The chapter ends with David ruling with justice and righteousness, and a list of his officials.

views.H: Traditional readers see the fulfillment of God's promise to subdue David's enemies (17:10), and the reach of David's kingdom to the Euphrates as the land promised to Abraham (Genesis 15:18).
views.C: Critical scholars debate the size of David's kingdom; many think the summary enlarges what may have been a smaller regional power, though few doubt that David fought the Arameans and Ammonites.
views.S: Compare 2 Samuel 8. Chronicles omits the execution of Moabite prisoners, names Gath for Metheg-ammah, agrees with 4QSam-a on the chariots, adds the bronze for the Temple (with the Greek of Samuel), credits Abishai in Edom, and changes "David's sons were priests" to chief officials.
views.X: Christian readers have seen in David's victories a picture of Christ's final victory over his enemies (Psalm 110:1; 1 Corinthians 15:25), while noting that Chronicles itself says David's wars disqualified him from building the Temple (22:8).

echoes: 2 Samuel 8:1–18; 1 Chronicles 17:10; 1 Chronicles 22:8; Genesis 15:18; 1 Kings 7:15–47; Psalm 60; 1 Kings 11:15–16

title: Insult and war with Ammon
sum: When Nahash of Ammon dies, David sends envoys to comfort his son Hanun. Hanun's officials say the envoys are spies, so Hanun shaves them, cuts their robes and sends them home in shame. Knowing they have made David their enemy, the Ammonites spend a thousand talents of silver to hire Aramean chariots and troops.

Joab, caught between two armies, splits his forces with Abishai and says, "Be strong... The LORD will do whatever he sees is good." The Arameans run, and so do the Ammonites. The Arameans gather again, with help from beyond the Euphrates, and David himself crosses the Jordan and defeats them. Hadadezer's vassals make peace, and Aram will not help Ammon again.

views.H: Traditional readers see a just war: David's kindness was met with insult, and his victory came from God, as Joab's words of faith show.
views.C: Critical scholars treat the Aramean wars as among the more historical parts of David's story, while noting that the numbers in both books have grown or been miscopied.
views.S: Compare 2 Samuel 10. Chronicles names Nahash, adds the thousand talents and the camp at Medeba, lists different allies, and has larger numbers: thirty-two thousand chariots (19:7) and seven thousand charioteers (19:18).
views.X: Christian readers often cite Joab's words in 19:13 as a model of courage joined with trust: do your duty, and leave the outcome to God.

settings.what: David's condolence and the Ammonite princes' charge
settings.to: Hanun son of Nahash, through David's envoys; then Hanun
settings.when: After the death of Nahash king of Ammon
settings.why: David means to keep 'loyal love' with Hanun as his father did with David. The princes call the envoys spies, and Hanun shames them. The misreading of a kind act starts the war that follows. Readers see that David's wars began with loyalty refused, not with his own greed.

settings.to: His brother Abshai, before the battle with Ammon and Aram
settings.when: Before the city of the Ammonites, facing enemies on two sides
settings.why: A plan of mutual help and a call to courage: 'Be strong... for the sake of our people and our God's cities. The LORD will do whatever he sees is good.' The words join bravery and trust. Chronicles copies them from 2 Samuel 10:11–12 almost word for word, and they fit its theme of fighting for God's people.

title: Rabbah and the giants
sum: In spring Joab leads the army against Ammon and besieges Rabbah, while David stays in Jerusalem. Joab takes the city; David takes the Ammonite king's crown, a talent of gold. In the Hebrew of Chronicles he cuts the people with saws and iron tools; Samuel's text speaks of forced labor (see the variant at 20:3). Then come three short reports of giants of Gath killed by David's men: Sippai by Sibbecai, Lahmi the brother of Goliath by Elhanan, and a man with six fingers and six toes by David's nephew Jonathan.

Between 20:1 and 20:2 lies the most famous gap in Chronicles. In Samuel, the words "David was staying in Jerusalem" open the story of Bathsheba and Uriah. Chronicles passes over it in silence and goes straight to Rabbah's fall.
readings: Many critical scholars since Wellhausen have seen the gap as proof that Chronicles cleaned up David's record, leaving out adultery, murder and family disaster.

Others answer that Chronicles assumes its readers know Samuel, as the abrupt shift from 20:1 to 20:2 shows, and that it tells David's reign as the story of the Temple's founder. That is why it includes the census of chapter 21, which was David's own sin and led to the Temple site, but not the private sins of his house.

views.H: Traditional readers hold that Chronicles, written for a people who already had Samuel, chose what served its purpose; it never denies what Samuel tells.
views.C: Critical scholars generally see a deliberate idealization of David and Solomon, though they debate how far it was meant to hide anything, since the readers knew Samuel.
views.S: Compare 2 Samuel 11:1; 2 Samuel 12:26–31; 2 Samuel 21:18–22. Chronicles skips Bathsheba, Uriah, Nathan's parable and Joab's message to David; reads "he sawed" for "he set"; places the first giant at Gezer; names Lahmi as Goliath's brother; and drops the giant who nearly killed David (2 Samuel 21:15–17).
views.J: The Talmud records a debate over David's sin. Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani, in the name of Rabbi Yonatan, argues that whoever says David sinned is mistaken, while Rav and others hold that David did wrong (Bavli Shabbat 56a). Neither side treats Chronicles' silence as a denial, and Psalm 51 has long been read as David's confession. The Targum on Samuel identified Elhanan with David.
views.X: Christian readers have often taken the contrast between the two books as a lesson in grace: Samuel shows David's sin, and Chronicles shows the same David as God's chosen builder, as if forgiven sin no longer defined him.

deep.b: 1 Samuel 17 says David killed Goliath of Gath. 2 Samuel 21:19 says Elhanan of Bethlehem killed Goliath the Gittite, whose spear shaft was like a weaver's beam. 1 Chronicles 20:5 says Elhanan killed Lahmi the brother of Goliath. The Hebrew of the two later verses is so close that one is likely a copy of the other, changed by accident or on purpose. Readers who think Chronicles is right see a damaged text in Samuel; readers who think Samuel is right see Chronicles harmonizing. A third, older answer, found in the Targum, says Elhanan was David. The site's 2 Samuel keeps its own Hebrew and shows Chronicles as a variant; here the Plain keeps Chronicles' Hebrew and shows Samuel. See the topic David and Goliath.

echoes: 2 Samuel 11:1; 2 Samuel 12:26–31; 2 Samuel 21:15–22; 1 Samuel 17:4–7; 1 Samuel 17:50; Psalm 51; 1 Chronicles 21:1–30
